teaser: A child holds a candle for an old man at work, and the light shines through small fingers.
review_notes:
Date about 1642 (Louvre: c. 1642). Size about 137 x 102 cm (54 x 40 in).
Given to the Louvre in 1948 by the English dealer Percy Moore Turner, in memory of curator Paul Jamot. Confirm.
It was found in England around 1938. Confirm.
Reading of the wooden beam and auger as a foreshadowing of the cross is the standard interpretation, not a documented statement by the artist.
Anecdote of Louis XIII removing all other paintings from his room to keep La Tour's Saint Sebastian comes from Dom Calmet (18th century); told as 'a story reports'.
La Tour held the title 'painter in ordinary to the king' by 1639.

lesson.text: The old man is strong, skilled and hard at work. The child is small and does nothing but hold a candle. So who is in charge here? Everything about the bodies says the man. Everything about the light says the child. Georges de La Tour leaves the two answers side by side.

The man is Joseph, the carpenter of Nazareth. The child is Jesus, perhaps eight or ten years old, helping in the workshop after dark. There are no halos, no angels, no golden rays. You could take it for any craftsman and any apprentice, in any village.

The canvas is about 137 centimeters high (54 inches), so the figures are close to life-size, and Joseph has to bend to fit inside it. His back fills the top of the picture like an arch. Under that arch, the only source of light is the flame.

lesson.title: Around the flame
lesson.text: Start at the candle and move outward, as the light does.

spots.title: The glowing hand
spots.text: The child shields the flame, and the light shines through the fingers, turning them red and almost transparent. Try it with a flashlight: La Tour had clearly watched this happen.

spots.title: The child's face
spots.text: The brightest thing in the painting, smooth as porcelain, with the lips parted. The child seems to be speaking, and the face gives off more light than the candle alone would explain.

spots.title: Joseph's forehead
spots.text: A bald skull, a furrowed brow, a gray beard, all in rough red-brown. He is not looking at his tool. His eyes are raised toward the child, and they look worried.

lesson.text: So the picture is a conversation. The old man works, the child talks, and the old man listens. In the 1600s this was read as the point: the one who seems to be the helper is the teacher, and his light is the kind you understand by.

A candle was not a small thing in the 1640s. Good ones were costly, most people worked by daylight and went to bed at dusk. A carpenter working late by a tall candle, with a child kept up to hold it, would have struck viewers as a scene of urgent labor.
Now look at what Joseph is actually making. La Tour could have shown him sawing or planing. He chose one particular action, with one particular shape of wood under the tool.
Two pieces of wood, drawn one after the other.

lines.label: The handle
lines.text: Joseph grips a horizontal wooden handle with both fists. It belongs to an auger, a large hand drill that you twist to bore a hole.

lines.label: The shaft
lines.text: The iron shaft drops straight down into a beam held under his foot. Handle and shaft together draw a cross, in the dark, right at the center of the workshop.

lines.label: The beam
lines.text: A heavy squared timber lies on the floor, and he is boring a hole through it. Viewers knew the end of the story: wood, nails and holes would return thirty years later.

lesson.text: La Tour hides the future inside an ordinary evening. Nothing supernatural is shown, yet the tools quietly announce the cross, and Joseph's anxious look suggests he half understands.

This is his method in the night pictures. He strips a religious subject of every traditional sign and trusts the light to carry the meaning. Shapes are simplified, colors reduced to browns, a dull red and the white of a shirt sleeve. The darkness removes everything that is not needed.

Joseph was a fashionable saint in La Tour's time. For centuries he had been a background figure, sometimes even a comic one. In the 1600s the Catholic Church promoted him as a model father and worker, and pictures of his workshop multiplied.

La Tour was no humble village painter. By 1639 he carried the title of painter to King Louis XIII. A story from the next century says the king liked one of his night scenes so much that he had every other painting taken out of his bedroom.
Somewhere on the floor is the proof that real carpentry is going on: a curl of wood, freshly cut. Can you spot it?

spots.title: The wood shaving
spots.text: A pale ribbon of wood, curled like a spring, lies near the child's sandal and catches a little light. La Tour observes it as carefully as the faces.

lesson.text: That shaving is typical of him: one humble, exact detail that makes the whole scene believable. Near it, in the gloom on the left, you can make out a chisel and a mallet. The holy story is set down among real tools.

The painting spent centuries unrecognized and turned up in England in the 1930s. An English art dealer, Percy Moore Turner, gave it to the Louvre in 1948, at a time when France had only recently rediscovered the forgotten painter from Lorraine.

Return to the question from the start. The man has the muscles, the tools and the years. The child has a candle and something to say. La Tour paints the old one bending down, and lets the light settle the matter.

quiz.question: What is the only source of light in the painting?
quiz.explanation: A single candle, shielded by the child's hand, lights the whole scene.

quiz.question: What tool is Joseph using?
options: An auger, a large hand drill
quiz.explanation: He twists an auger into a beam held under his foot.

quiz.question: What do the handle and shaft of the tool suggest?
quiz.explanation: Together they draw a cross, announcing the end of the story.

quiz.question: What happens to the child's hand in front of the flame?
options: It casts a shadow on Joseph
The light glows through the fingers
It is hidden by a sleeve
quiz.explanation: The fingers turn red and nearly transparent.

quiz.question: Which king did La Tour serve as painter?
quiz.explanation: He held the title of painter to King Louis XIII by 1639.

facts.text: Jesus and Joseph are shown with golden halos.
facts.explanation: La Tour removes every traditional holy sign and lets the light carry the meaning.

facts.text: Joseph looks toward the child instead of at his work.
facts.explanation: His eyes are raised to the child, with a worried expression.

facts.text: The painting has been in the Louvre since the 1600s.
facts.explanation: It was given to the museum in 1948 by an English art dealer.
